h1: The 8 Best Clix-Style Gaming Keyboards in 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 compact 60% and 65% gaming keyboards in the competitive style, scored on switches, latency, layout and price from under $30.
summary: The AULA WIN68 HE is the keyboard to buy if you want the competitive edge, with Hall effect magnetic switches, adjustable actuation down to 0.02 mm and an 8,000 Hz polling rate. The HITIME M67 is the best wireless, hot-swappable board, the Redragon K671 is the best cheap board you can modify, and the surmen 65% is the best simple linear option under $30.
intro: Search for Clix keyboards and you find the same thing everywhere: small boards, red switches, glowing keycaps. The part that gets skipped is why that style took over competitive Fortnite. A compact layout leaves room to swing the mouse wide, and a fast, light switch lets you edit and build with less finger travel. The brand on the box matters far less than those two traits, and none of the boards here is endorsed by or tied to any player.

So this ranking is about the style, not a name. We reviewed eight compact keyboards from the listings and spec sheets, sorting them by switch technology, response claims, layout, connectivity and how much you can customize. Where a listing gives marketing language instead of a number, such as a membrane board calling itself mechanical-feeling, we say so plainly.

products.name: AULA WIN68 HE Mechanical Gaming Keyboard 60%, Hall Effect Magnetic Switch, Fast Trigger Mode Adjustable Actuation, 8000Hz Polling Rate, RGB Backlit, Wired Black Keyboard for Laptop/PC Gamer
products.verdict: A Hall effect board with rapid trigger and 8,000 Hz polling for under $50.
products.description:
The WIN68 HE is a 68-key wired board with magnetic Hall effect switches. Actuation can be set anywhere from 0.02 mm to 3.44 mm in 0.1 mm steps, press and reset sensitivity are adjustable per key, and the listing claims an 8,000 Hz polling rate with 0.3 ms latency. Lighting is 16.8 million color RGB, and the USB cable detaches.

It wins because it is the only pick whose switches are fundamentally different from the rest. Magnetic switches read key depth continuously, so rapid trigger can reset the instant you lift, which is the mechanism behind the fast stop-and-strafe feel competitive players chase. The red-switch boards below simply cannot do that. The arrow keys also stay on a 68-key layout, unlike the 61-key boards.

Buy it if you play ranked and want tunable input for $30 to $50. The caveat is software: the web driver for remapping runs on Windows only, so Mac users lose most of the tuning.
products.idealFor: Competitive players who want to tune every key's trigger point.
products.skipIf: You use a Mac or want a wireless board.

products.name: HITIME x XVX M67 Wireless 60% Percent Keyboard, VIA Topographic Gaming Keyboard, Tri-Mode Thocky Creamy Mechanical Key Board, Hot Swappable Gasket Mount RGB IMD Tech for Win/Mac(JadeStone)
products.verdict: Tri-mode wireless with a gasket mount, hot-swap sockets and VIA remapping.
products.description:
The M67 connects by Bluetooth 5.0, a 2.4 GHz dongle or Type-C wired, and pairs with five devices on a 4,000 mAh battery. It uses a gasket mount with a slotted PCB and four layers of damping foam, pre-lubed transparent linear switches rated for 80 million keystrokes, hot-swap sockets for 3-pin and 5-pin switches, and VIA remapping that works on Windows, macOS and Linux.

It takes second place because it is the most complete board for the money, but it is a lifestyle board before a pure competitive one. Wireless adds latency risk over a cable, and the 2.4 GHz mode is the one to use for play. Against the AULA it trades Hall effect precision for the ability to swap switches, a softer typing feel and a battery. Remapping is only possible while wired, a quirk to note.

Buy it for a desk that doubles as a work setup. The caveat is that nothing on the listing states a polling rate or latency number.
pros: VIA works on every major OS
products.idealFor: Players who also use the board for work and want to customize.
products.skipIf: You want the lowest possible input latency.

products.name: Redragon Mechanical Gaming Keyboard Wired, 11 Programmable Backlit Modes, Hot-Swappable Red Switch, Anti-Ghosting, Double-Shot PBT Keycaps, Light Up Keyboard for PC Mac
products.verdict: A hot-swappable linear board with spare switches and macro software for under $30.
products.description:
The Redragon K671 uses hot-swappable linear red switches, ships with four spare switches and two red keycaps, and supports macro editing and key remapping through software. It has 11 backlight modes with five brightness levels, double-shot keycaps and 12 multimedia shortcuts. The listing's width of about 17 inches makes it a wider board than the 60 and 65 percent options here.

It ranks third because it is the cheapest board with swappable switches and spare parts, so a dead switch costs a few seconds, not a keyboard. The tradeoff is footprint. At roughly 17 inches wide it takes far more desk than the compact boards, and a tight mouse space is the whole reason the Clix style spread. The keycaps are described as double-shot ABS in one place and the listing leaves the PBT question open.

Buy it if desk space is not a problem and you want a proper full set of keys. Skip it if you play on low sensitivity with a wide mouse sweep.
products.idealFor: Budget buyers who want to learn switch swapping.
products.skipIf: You need a compact layout for wide mouse sweeps.

products.name: surmen 65% Percent Gaming Keyboard Mechanical with Linear Red Switch, 68-Keys Pink Mini Gaming Keyboard 60 Percent LED Light Backlit PBT Keycaps for Laptop Desktop PC Gamers (68 Miami)
products.verdict: A 68-key linear board with dedicated arrows and PBT keycaps for under $30.
products.description:
The surmen is a wired 65 percent board with 68 keys, linear red switches, double-injection PBT keycaps with shine-through legends, full anti-ghosting and two-stage adjustable tilt legs. It works with Windows, Mac and Linux, and the listing says the backlight can be turned off.

It ranks fourth because the layout keeps the arrow keys that the 61-key boards drop, which matters in games and in daily typing. Against the Redragon it is smaller and uses PBT keycaps that resist shine, but it has no hot-swap sockets, so a worn switch means a fresh board. The 50 million keystroke figure is a maker claim and the listing says nothing about polling rate or software.

This is the right buy for a first compact board when you want the light linear feel without paying more. The caveat is that there is no software at all: lighting is a single effect with shortcut keys only.
products.idealFor: First-time compact board buyers on a tight budget.
products.skipIf: You want to remap keys or swap switches.

products.name: Snpurdiri 60% Wired Mechanical Keyboard (Black-Red, Red Switches) | Mini Gaming Keyboard with 61 Keys for PC, Windows XP, Win 7, Win 10
products.verdict: A pocket-sized 61-key board with a swappable USB-C cable.
products.description:
The Snpurdiri is a 60 percent wired board with 61 keys, red switches, rainbow LED backlighting, two feet for tilt adjustment and a detachable USB-C cable. The listed dimensions are about 11.4 by 4 by 1.5 inches, which makes it the smallest board in this ranking.

It places fifth because it is the one to bag for a LAN event or a laptop desk, and the detachable cable is a real advantage: a frayed cord on a fixed-cable board kills the keyboard, while here it costs a few dollars. Compared with the surmen it drops the arrow keys and the PBT keycaps, which the listing does not mention, and it has no hot-swap sockets. The compatibility list stops at Windows, with no mention of Mac.

Buy it if size is your top concern and the budget is under $30. The caveat is that nothing on the listing gives a polling or latency figure, and the missing arrow keys sit on a function layer.
products.idealFor: Players who travel or have a very small desk.
products.skipIf: You want arrow keys on the main layer.

products.name: iTastatur 60 Percent Gaming Keyboard Mechanical with Linear Red Switch, 60% Wired Ultra-Compact Mini Keyboard LED with PBT Keycaps for Ps4/Ps5/Xbox（61 Miami）
products.verdict: A 61-key linear board with PBT keycaps and console support at a low price.
products.description:
The iTastatur is a 61-key wired board with linear red switches, double-shot PBT keycaps, an LED backlight, a double kickstand and n-key rollover. The listing states compatibility with Windows, Mac, and consoles including the PS4, PS5 and Xbox.

It ranks sixth because the combination of PBT and a console claim is useful for players who split time between a PC and a console. Compared with the surmen, it drops the arrow keys, and compared with the Snpurdiri it does not list a detachable cable. The odd phrasing about drive distance on the listing is unclear, so we do not credit any switch travel figure. Whether a given console accepts a USB keyboard for in-game input varies by title, so check your game first.

Choose it for a small-footprint board that also sits at the console. The caveat: the listing leaves out polling rate, cable type and software support.
cons: No arrow keys on main layer
products.idealFor: Players who share a board between PC and console.
products.skipIf: You need a detachable cable or remapping.

products.name: Ussixchare 60 Percent Gaming Keyboard 61 Keys Wired Mechanical Keyboard Ultra Compact Keyboard Red Switch LED Backlit for Windows Laptop Gamer(61 Miami)
products.verdict: A 61-key board with 18 backlight modes, priced above the near-identical iTastatur.
products.description:
The Ussixchare is a wired 60 percent board with 61 keys, red switches, PBT keycaps, full-key rollover and 18 backlight modes with static, breathing and reactive effects. It lists support for Windows, consoles and multiple systems, and its listed width is about 14 inches.

It ranks seventh because it sits at $30 to $50, more than the similar iTastatur and Snpurdiri, for a spec sheet with no meaningful advantage beyond lighting. The listing describes red switches as tactile, which is wrong: red switches are linear, so treat that description with caution. An 18-mode light show does not improve your aim. It matters more that the listing says nothing about cable type, software or hot-swap sockets.

Buy it only if you want the extra lighting modes. The caveat is value: the cheaper boards above deliver the same layout and switch type for less.
products.idealFor: Buyers who put lighting effects first.
products.skipIf: You are comparing on switch quality or value.

products.name: GEODMAER 65% Gaming Keyboard, Wired Backlit Mini Keyboard, Ultra-Compact Anti-Ghosting No-Conflict 68 Keys Membrane Gaming Wired Keyboard for PC Laptop Windows Gamer
products.verdict: A membrane board with mechanical-style feel for the quietest, cheapest compact layout.
products.description:
The GEODMAER is a 65 percent, 68-key board with a detachable Type-C cable and 11 media buttons. It is a membrane keyboard that imitates the feel of a mechanical one, with a claimed 10 million keystroke life, two-color injection keycaps with a UV coating, a Win key lock and a listed 26-key no-conflict rating.

It lands last because the Clix-style appeal is switch speed, and a membrane board cannot offer the actuation feel of any board above it. The 26-key conflict figure is also far below the n-key rollover listed on the others, which can matter when you press many keys at once. The upside is price and noise: it is the quietest option here, with a detachable cable and a Win key lock.

Buy it as a stopgap or office keyboard that also games a bit. Skip it for ranked play, and note that the listing gives no polling rate or software.
products.idealFor: Casual players who want a compact, quiet keyboard.
products.skipIf: You play ranked or want true mechanical switches.

methodology.title: Switch technology
methodology.description: We compared Hall effect, hot-swappable linear and fixed red switches, with membrane boards scored lower for competitive use.

methodology.title: Latency and polling claims
methodology.description: Stated polling rates and latency figures were credited only when the listing gave a number, and always treated as maker claims.

methodology.title: Layout and footprint
methodology.description: 60, 65 and wider layouts were compared for desk space against the keys you lose.

methodology.title: Connectivity and software
methodology.description: Wired, wireless and detachable cables were weighed alongside remapping software and operating system support.

methodology.title: Keycaps, build and price
methodology.description: PBT versus ABS keycaps, mounting style and price bracket were scored against what each listing actually states.

whatMatters.detail: A linear switch moves smoothly with no bump, which suits repeated fast presses. Hall effect switches use magnets to read depth, so the actuation point can be moved and a rapid trigger can reset the instant you release. Look for the words Hall effect or magnetic on a listing, as on the AULA WIN68 HE, and treat plain red switch as a fixed linear.

Actuation is how far a key must travel to register. A short, adjustable point lets you act sooner but risks accidental inputs. The AULA lists a range of 0.02 to 3.44 mm, while ordinary red switches have a fixed point. Check whether the listing says adjustable, and whether you can set press and reset separately.

A 60 percent board has 61 keys and no arrow cluster, a 65 percent board adds arrows with 68 keys, and wider boards add more. Smaller means more room for the mouse arm, which is the main reason the compact style took over competitive play. Match the layout to how much you use arrow keys, and measure your desk.

A cable gives the steadiest signal and lowest latency, and a detachable one saves the keyboard if the cord frays. Wireless adds convenience, and the HITIME M67 offers both Bluetooth and 2.4 GHz modes. For play, use the 2.4 GHz or wired mode and keep Bluetooth for work.

PBT keycaps resist shine and wear better than ABS, and double-shot caps keep their legends. Hot-swap sockets let you change switches without soldering, as on the HITIME and Redragon. Look for the words PBT, double-shot and hot-swappable on the listing, and remember that software remapping may be limited by operating system.

faq.q: Does this list reflect what Clix actually uses?
faq.a: No. We make no claim about any player's gear, and none of these brands is endorsed by or tied to one. The list covers the compact, fast-switch style associated with competitive Fortnite play.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake buyers make?
faq.a: Chasing lighting and keycap colors instead of the switch and layout. The AULA WIN68 HE costs about the same as the Ussixchare yet offers adjustable actuation. Decide on switch type and size first, then choose a color.

faq.q: Is the AULA worth it over a standard red-switch board?
faq.a: For ranked play, yes. Hall effect switches let you set actuation and reset per key, which a fixed red switch like the surmen cannot. For casual play, the extra tuning is not needed and a cheaper board does fine.

faq.q: How do I set up a hot-swappable board?
faq.a: Pull the keycap, then use a switch puller to lift the old switch out of its socket and press a new one straight in. The HITIME M67 takes 3-pin and 5-pin switches, and the Redragon includes four spares.

faq.q: How do I look after a compact keyboard?
faq.a: Pull the keycaps now and then and clear dust with a soft brush. On PBT boards like the surmen, a damp cloth is fine. Keep drinks away, since most of these boards have no spill protection listed.

faq.q: Will the AULA software work on a Mac?
faq.a: No. The listing says the web driver does not support macOS, so remapping and rapid trigger setup need Windows. If you use a Mac, the HITIME M67 with VIA is the better choice.

finalTake: If you want the real competitive edge, buy the AULA WIN68 HE and spend an evening tuning actuation. The HITIME M67 is the best board if you want wireless and a custom feel, and the Redragon K671 is the cheapest way to learn switch swapping. Avoid paying more for lighting modes, and skip the membrane GEODMAER for ranked play. Switch, layout and connection matter far more than the name attached to the style.
